title: The Sage of Nininger: A Sunken Continent, a Comet, a Cipher, and the Preamble at Omaha
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Moyamensing: The Physician's Son and the Bar

stops.name: Moyamensing, Philadelphia, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and city from Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly', which gives only that the father was an immigrant from Fintona, County Tyrone, and that the mother kept a pawn shop. The father's title of physician and the parents' full names come from MNopedia, 'Donnelly, Ignatius (1831-1901)'. Moyamensing is a district-level location; no street address was found. Coordinates are the district center per Wikipedia, 'Moyamensing, Philadelphia'.
stops.campa: On the third of November a son is born in Moyamensing, the Irish district of Philadelphia lying south of South Street toward the Delaware, to Philip Carroll Donnelly and Catherine Gavin Donnelly. The father is a physician. The mother keeps a pawn shop, and it is the pawn shop that carries the household after he is gone. They name the boy for the founder of the Jesuits: Ignatius Loyola Donnelly. He grows up among dockhands and immigrants, in a ward of cheap rents and hard ward politics, a few streets back from the wharves.
suggested_refs: The Moyamensing district of Philadelphia, bounded by South Street, the Delaware, and Seventeenth Street

stops.name: Juniper Street, Central High School
stops.date_confidence: attested that he attended Central High School and studied under John S. Hart (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); no source checked gives the years of attendance, so the date is an ordering device only. Coordinates are the 1838-1854 building on the east side of Juniper Street below Market, per Wikipedia, 'Central High School (Philadelphia)'.
stops.campa: He is admitted to Central High School, then on the east side of Juniper Street below Market, the second public high school founded in the United States. His master is John S. Hart, who drills the boys in rhetoric, grammar, and the writing of verse, and the training takes. The habit of argument by accumulation, evidence heaped until the heap itself persuades, is fixed in him here. In September 1854 the school moves to a new building at Broad and Green. Donnelly has been gone from it for years by then.
suggested_refs: John S. Hart's textbooks of rhetoric and composition, used at Central High School in the 1840s

stops.name: Philadelphia, The Mourner's Vision
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year from the bibliography in Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; month and day unknown and defaulted. No sales or reception figures were found for the poem.
stops.campa: At nineteen he publishes his first work, a poem called The Mourner's Vision. Everything he makes afterward is the work of a man who began as a poet: the land circulars, the campaign speeches, the twelve propositions about a drowned continent, the novel published under another man's name. The verse itself is of its period, grand and mournful, addressed to nations rather than to persons, and nobody reads it now except for the sake of who wrote it. It goes out from a Philadelphia press in 1850 and he is nineteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Mourner's Vision (Philadelphia, 1850), Donnelly's first published book

stops.name: Philadelphia, Brewster's office and the bar
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict on the year of admission: Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly' gives 1852; MNopedia gives 1853. Not resolved here; the earlier date is used to order the segment. The clerkship with Benjamin Brewster is [R], carried by Wikipedia without a document behind it. Coordinates are the old city center of Philadelphia, not an office address.
stops.campa: He reads law in the office of Benjamin Harris Brewster, a Philadelphia lawyer who will end his career as Attorney General of the United States, and is admitted to the Pennsylvania bar. The practice he sets up is ordinary work: conveyances, small suits, and the land speculation that in this decade is nearly everyone's second trade. He will carry both instruments west, the lawyer's brief and the speculator's prospectus, and he will use them on the same ground. The year of the admission is 1852 by one account of his life and 1853 by another, and the two have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: The rolls of the Pennsylvania bar for 1852 and 1853, which would settle the conflict between Wikipedia and MNopedia

stops.name: Philadelphia, marriage and the stump
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for both the marriage to Katherine McCaffrey and the resignation of the legal clerkship for Democratic campaign speaking (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); month and day unknown and defaulted. The rumor of financial scandal preceding the move west is reported by Wikipedia without particulars and is not independently attested.
stops.campa: He marries Katherine McCaffrey, who will bear three children and outlast nearly forty years of his campaigns, and in the same season he gives up a legal clerkship to speak for the Democrats on the stump. The stump suits him. A crowd is a jury that cannot adjourn, and he learns in the Philadelphia wards what he will use for the rest of his life: an audience will follow a long chain of assertions if the man making them never once appears to doubt. Two years later he is in Minnesota, with talk of money mishandled behind him.
suggested_refs: Philadelphia ward politics of the mid-1850s, the school of his platform manner

segments.name: Nininger City: The Town Sold in Advance

stops.name: St. Paul, up the river into the Territory
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The move to Minnesota Territory in 1857 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; MNopedia); the arrival by steamboat at the St. Paul levee is the standard route of the year and is not separately documented for Donnelly. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes up the Mississippi to St. Paul in 1857, the ordinary route for an eastern man with capital and reasons for leaving. Minnesota is still a Territory, statehood a year off, and the whole upper river is being sold in lots by men who have never walked over them. He arrives holding a license to practice law and the conviction that a city can be founded the way a firm is founded. What follows him out of Philadelphia is talk of money handled badly, never proved and never quite dropped. He comes off the boat at the lower levee, under the bluff, with his wife beside him.
suggested_refs: The St. Paul lower levee, landing of the 1857 immigration into Minnesota Territory

stops.name: Nininger City, the partnership and the promotion
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction to the usual telling. Wikipedia, 'Nininger, Minnesota' states the town was founded and named by John Nininger, brother-in-law of Governor Alexander Ramsey, and incorporated in the winter of 1857-58; MNopedia has Donnelly partnering with Nininger to promote the townsite. Donnelly is therefore promoter and partner from 1857, not co-founder. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Fifteen miles downriver, on the Dakota County bank above Hastings, John Nininger has laid out a townsite and given it his own name. Donnelly comes in as partner and promoter, and the promotion is the town: engraved views of a levee, a mill, and streets that do not yet exist, mailed east to men who will buy a lot they have never seen. Nininger City sells. By the spring of 1858 something near a thousand people are living in it, and Donnelly, twenty-six years old, is the public voice of a model community.
suggested_refs: The Nininger City townsite plat and its engraved promotional views, 1857

stops.name: Nininger, the emigrant circulars
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The founding and promotion effort is attested (Wikipedia, 'Nininger, Minnesota'); the promotional writing is inferred from it and not separately sourced. An earlier draft of this material dated the circulars to 1856, which is impossible: Donnelly did not reach Minnesota Territory until 1857.
stops.campa: From Nininger he writes the literature that sells it: circulars and emigrant appeals promising eastern families a city on the Mississippi where land is cheap, the society improving, and the future certain. It is the first sustained prose of his life after the poem, and it fixes the method. He is not describing a place falsely; he is describing it accurately in advance, and expecting the description to bring the place about. Households in Pennsylvania and New York read the circular and begin to pack.
suggested_refs: The Emigrant Aid Journal of Nininger, the townsite's promotional organ

stops.name: Nininger, the Panic of 1857
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Panic of 1857 collapsed the venture and left Donnelly heavily indebted, and that the population, which had approached a thousand, drained away (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; Wikipedia, 'Nininger, Minnesota'; MNopedia). Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Panic reaches the upper river within months of the sale. Eastern credit stops, the lots become unsalable, the buyers do not come, and the families already in Nininger begin to go out the way they came in. Donnelly is left holding land nobody wants and debts he will carry for years. He does not leave. He stays on in it, farming and borrowing and writing, for the remaining forty-four years of his life. The town empties around him street by platted street.
suggested_refs: The Panic of 1857 on the upper Mississippi and the collapse of the Minnesota townsite boom

stops.name: Dakota County, two defeats at the polls
stops.date_confidence: attested that he ran unsuccessfully for the Minnesota state legislature in 1857 and again in 1858 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'), which gives no districts, opponents, or margins. Month is an ordering device. The characterization of his constituency is inference from the documented Panic and from his later Anti-Monopoly politics.
stops.campa: He runs for the Minnesota legislature in 1857 and loses, runs again in 1858 and loses again. The county is full of ruined speculators and he is the most conspicuous of them. What he takes away from the two defeats is the audience: farmers with mortgages, storekeepers with unpaid ledgers, men who watched eastern money arrive, raise the price of everything, and withdraw. He will speak to that constituency for the next forty years, and in 1860 it puts him on a state ticket.
suggested_refs: Minnesota Territorial and early state election returns, 1857 and 1858

stops.name: Nininger, the farmhouse and the library
stops.date_confidence: attested that he remained at Nininger for the rest of his life in a large farmhouse surrounded by fields and was known as the Sage of Nininger (MNopedia). The contents of the library and the reading habit are reconstruction from the source apparatus of the books he wrote there. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The farmhouse stands among fields where the streets of the paper city were to run. Here he raises his children, farms without much attention, and reads: geology, comparative mythology, the classical authors, the reports of government surveys, whatever the mails carry to a river town in Dakota County. Every book he publishes over the next thirty years is assembled in this house, out of printed sources, by a man with no excavation and no university behind him. The neighbors call him the Sage of Nininger, half in affection and half not.
suggested_refs: The plaque marking Donnelly's former residence at Nininger, and the plaque at Good Templars Hall

segments.name: Wabasha Hill and the War Congress

stops.name: St. Paul, Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota
stops.date_confidence: attested that he served as Lieutenant Governor from 1860 to 1863 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); month and day of taking office not given by the source and defaulted. Coordinates are the first Minnesota capitol on Wabasha Hill, in use 1854-1881, NOT the 1905 building at 44.9553, -93.1022, which several compilations wrongly attach to his legislative service.
stops.campa: At twenty-eight the bankrupt promoter out of the emptied town takes office as Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota, second in the government of the state, a Republican now. The first capitol stands on Wabasha Hill, a plain building above the river that will burn in 1881. He presides over the state Senate there through the opening years of the Civil War, and through the Dakota War fought in the state's own west in 1862. The term runs from 1860 to 1863.
suggested_refs: The first Minnesota State Capitol on Wabasha Hill, St. Paul, burned 1 March 1881

stops.name: Washington, the seat in the war Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested; he took his seat for Minnesota's 2nd district in the 38th Congress on 4 March 1863 and served through the 40th (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). The detail about his use of Washington libraries is reconstruction from the scale of the source apparatus in his later books; the Library of Congress in these years sat inside the Capitol's west front, not in the Jefferson Building, which opened in 1897.
stops.campa: He takes his seat for Minnesota's second district in the 38th Congress. The dome above him is newly finished and the war under it is not. He speaks for the northwestern farmer and for the railroads that will carry the farmer's wheat, two positions that sit together comfortably in 1863 and will not sit together for long. Washington also supplies what Nininger cannot: libraries, survey reports, the printed findings of men sent out to measure the continent. He reads in the Capitol's west front, where the Library then is.
suggested_refs: The Library of Congress in its rooms in the west front of the Capitol, its home until 1897

stops.name: Washington, the Freedmen's Bureau and the suffrage vote
stops.date_confidence: attested that as a Radical Republican he backed the Freedmen's Bureau and women's suffrage (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); the source gives no roll calls or dates, so the date here orders the 39th Congress and nothing more.
stops.campa: Through the 39th Congress he votes with the Radicals: for the Freedmen's Bureau, for the reconstruction of the defeated South on terms the defeated do not choose, for the enfranchisement of the freedmen. The faculty that will make him ridiculous twenty years later, the willingness to hold a position no respectable person holds, is at this date indistinguishable from courage. He speaks for women's suffrage besides, which in 1866 is a thing a man says in order to be laughed at, and he goes on saying it.
suggested_refs: The Congressional Globe for the 39th Congress, which would supply the roll calls the secondary sources omit

stops.name: Washington, the seat lost
stops.date_confidence: attested that his congressional service ended 3 March 1869 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). The particulars of the quarrel with the Minnesota Republican machine and with the Ramsey faction are widely repeated in accounts of his career but are not documented in the sources checked this session; treat that sentence as [R].
stops.campa: His third term ends on the third of March, and his Republican career ends with it. He has fallen out with the Minnesota party machine, with the faction around Alexander Ramsey, and with the railroad interest he once accommodated, and the nomination goes elsewhere. The next twenty years he will spend running for things, mostly as the candidate of whatever new party the farmers have just finished making. He is thirty-seven, out of office, and back in a house in a town of a few dozen people. He never holds federal office again.
suggested_refs: The Minnesota Republican nominating conventions of 1868, where the second district seat was lost to him

stops.name: St. Paul, the Anti-Monopolist founded
stops.date_confidence: attested: MNopedia states he founded the Anti-Monopolist, a party newspaper, at St. Paul in 1874. An earlier pass flagged this as unverified reconstruction; the flag is withdrawn. Month and day unknown and defaulted. The description of its editorial content is inference from the paper's title and the politics of the Grange years.
stops.campa: He founds a newspaper at St. Paul and calls it the Anti-Monopolist, which is the entire program in one word. He writes most of it himself, in the voice he has been sharpening since the emigrant circulars, and the Grange readers who take it in are the beginning of something that will outgrow the state entirely. Its enemy is the railroad: the elevator combine, the freight rate fixed in Chicago that decides what a bushel of Minnesota wheat is worth, the legislature that will not touch either of them.
suggested_refs: Surviving files of the Anti-Monopolist, St. Paul, in the Minnesota Historical Society newspaper collection

stops.name: St. Paul, the state Senate in the Grange years
stops.date_confidence: attested; elected to the Minnesota Senate for the 20th district, serving from 6 January 1874 to 6 January 1879 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). Coordinates are the first capitol on Wabasha Hill, which stood until the fire of 1 March 1881; the frequently cited 44.9537, -93.1028 is the 1905 building and is anachronistic for every Donnelly legislative stop.
stops.campa: He returns to the capitol on Wabasha Hill, this time to the state Senate, elected out of the farmer revolt his own paper is helping to organize. The Grange has swept the upper Midwest and the demand is everywhere the same: regulate the roads, break the rate. Between sessions he is at Nininger with the mails and the books, and the two occupations, the legislative and the antiquarian, run beside each other for the rest of his life without either one explaining the other. He serves in the Senate from January 1874 to January 1879.
suggested_refs: The Granger laws of the upper Midwest and the Minnesota railroad-rate legislation of the 1870s

stops.name: Minnesota, the crowd of ten thousand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, deliberately downgraded. Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly' states verbatim that in 1877 he spoke to a meeting of ten thousand where he read his preamble to the People's Party conference platform. That is anachronistic: the People's Party did not exist until 1891-92 and his famous preamble is the Omaha Platform preamble of 4 July 1892. His 1877 vehicle was the Anti-Monopoly and Greenback movement. The crowd and the preamble-reading are kept, the party name is dropped. Location within Minnesota is not given by the source; the pin is St. Paul. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He reads a preamble to a crowd the newspapers put at ten thousand: an indictment of monopoly, of the money power, and of a Republic whose government has been taken away from the people who made it. The vehicle in 1877 is the Anti-Monopoly and Greenback agitation. The party that will carry this language to a national convention does not exist yet and will not for another fifteen years. He has the paragraph a long time before he has the party to put it in.
suggested_refs: The Greenback and Anti-Monopoly platforms of the Minnesota agitation of the 1870s

stops.name: Nininger, writing Atlantis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to place. No source specifies where the book was composed; it is inferred from his continuous residence at Nininger from 1857 (MNopedia). The book itself and its argument are attested (Wikipedia, 'Atlantis: The Antediluvian World'). Date is an ordering device before the 1882 publication.
stops.campa: In the farmhouse he writes the book. The argument is old and the assembly is new: Plato's account of a great island beyond the Pillars of Hercules, sunk in a day and a night, is not a moral fable but a record, and every flood story, every pyramid, every shared god and shared word on the two shores of the Atlantic is debris from it. He works from printed sources alone, cross-ruled and indexed, comparative mythology on one side of the desk and the new geology and philology on the other.
stops.quote: Plato has preserved for us the history of Atlantis. If our views are correct, it is one of the most valuable records which have come down to us from antiquity.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Chapter II, 'Plato's History of Atlantis', opening (Project Gutenberg ebook 4032)
suggested_refs: Plato, Timaeus and Critias, the sole ancient source for Atlantis and the whole foundation of Donnelly's case
sources: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882), Project Gutenberg ebook 4032

stops.name: Nininger, Kircher's map among the evidence
stops.date_confidence: the map is attested. Athanasius Kircher's map of Atlantis in Mundus Subterraneus (1665) exists and is a documented early modern attempt to place the island geographically. That Donnelly used it is [R] as sourced this session, though the map is reproduced in editions of Atlantis. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Among the evidence he gathers is a map of Atlantis engraved by Athanasius Kircher two centuries earlier, the island drawn between Spain and America with south at the top, which the Jesuit said he had from Egyptian sources. The compilation works this way throughout: a seventeenth-century speculative chart, a deep-sea sounding from the Challenger expedition, a Mayan codex, a Norse flood story, all admitted on the same footing, as witnesses who could not have arranged their testimony together. He puts the map into the book, south still at the top of it.
stops.quote: That the description of this island given by Plato is not, as has been long supposed, fable, but veritable history.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Chapter I, 'The Purpose of the Book', Proposition 2 (Project Gutenberg ebook 4032)
suggested_refs: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus Subterraneus (Amsterdam, 1665), and its map 'Situs Insulae Atlantidis'
sources: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882), Project Gutenberg ebook 4032

stops.name: Franklin Square, New York, Harper and Brothers publish Atlantis
stops.date_confidence: attested; Harper and Brothers published Atlantis: The Antediluvian World in 1882 and it was a commercial success (Wikipedia, 'Atlantis: The Antediluvian World'). Month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinates are Franklin Square at Pearl, Dover, and Cherry Streets, where the Harper buildings stood, per Wikipedia, 'Franklin Square (Manhattan)'.
stops.campa: Harper and Brothers publish Atlantis: The Antediluvian World from Franklin Square, and it sells, and goes on selling. A bankrupt promoter from an emptied Minnesota town has written a bestseller. The readers who take it hardest are not the geologists. Helena Blavatsky's Theosophists absorb the drowned continent whole into their cosmology of root races, and Augustus Le Plongeon, two years later and fresh from digging at Chichen Itza, places his own lost continent of Mu in the Atlantic in explicit agreement with it.
stops.quote: This book is an attempt to demonstrate several distinct and novel propositions.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Chapter I, 'The Purpose of the Book', opening sentence (Project Gutenberg ebook 4032)
suggested_refs: Helena Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine (1888), which carries the Atlantean root-race doctrine into Theosophy
Augustus Le Plongeon, Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx (1896)
sources: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882), Project Gutenberg ebook 4032

stops.name: Nininger, Ragnarok and the age of fire and gravel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); the publisher was D. Appleton and Company of New York, per Wikipedia, 'Ragnarok: The Age of Fire and Gravel' and Open Library edition records, not Harper and Brothers as some compilations state. No sales or reception figures are attested for Ragnarok; claims that it sold as well as Atlantis are [R]. Composition at Nininger is inferred, as with Atlantis.
stops.campa: The sequel argues that the gravel and clay spread over the northern hemisphere, which the geologists explain by ice, were dropped by the tail of a comet that struck the earth within human memory, and that the fire, the darkness, and the flood in the myths of every people are eyewitness testimony to that day. It is the argument of Atlantis built a second time: the myths are true, and they are describing something. Ragnarok is the more loosely reasoned of the two and the one its author loves better. D. Appleton and Company publish it in New York in 1883.
stops.quote: That Atlantis perished in a terrible convulsion of nature, in which the whole island sunk into the ocean, with nearly all its inhabitants.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Chapter I, Proposition 12, the catastrophe thesis Ragnarok extends to the whole earth (Project Gutenberg ebook 4032)
suggested_refs: Ragnarok: The Age of Fire and Gravel (New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1883)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ragnarok: The Age of Fire and Gravel'
Open Library edition records for Ragnarok

stops.name: Nininger, The Shakespeare Myth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year from the bibliography in Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; month and day unknown, and the month here orders the stop after the January election. The summary of the Baconian case is standard and is attested at Wikipedia, 'Baconian theory'.
stops.campa: He publishes The Shakespeare Myth, a short first statement of the case: that the plays cannot have been written by a Stratford grain dealer with no education, no library, no Latin, and no record of ever owning a book, and that they were written by Francis Bacon. The argument is not his invention. What is his is what he means to do with it: prove it not by literary judgment, which he distrusts, but arithmetically, out of the printed page itself, where taste has no vote. The pamphlet states the case. It does not yet contain the proof.
suggested_refs: Delia Bacon and the earlier nineteenth-century anti-Stratfordians, on whose case Donnelly builds

stops.name: St. Paul, the House seat as an Independent
stops.date_confidence: attested; elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives for the 25th district as an Independent, serving 3 January 1887 to 6 January 1889 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). Coordinates are the second capitol, completed 1883 on the first capitol's Wabasha Hill site, not the 1905 building.
stops.campa: He is returned to the Minnesota House, now as an Independent from the twenty-fifth district, the party label having become for him a convenience of the season. Farmers' Alliance, Anti-Monopoly, Greenback, Independent, Populist: he stands under each in turn and says very nearly the same thing under all of them. In the same winter he is at work on a cipher, counting words forward and backward through the columns of the 1623 Folio in a farmhouse on the Mississippi.
suggested_refs: The second Minnesota State Capitol, built 1883 on the Wabasha Hill site of the first

stops.name: Chicago, The Great Cryptogram
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and publisher: R. S. Peale and Company, Chicago, 1888, per Open Library edition records and Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'. Coordinates are a city-level pin for Chicago, not the publisher's street address, which was not found this session. Bacon's biliteral cipher is separately attested from Bacon's own De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623).
stops.campa: R. S. Peale and Company of Chicago publish The Great Cryptogram in two volumes, near a thousand pages. Francis Bacon had in fact devised a real cipher, the biliteral, one letter concealed in the shape of five, and Donnelly takes that for a license to look for another. The method is his own and it is arithmetical: a root number, operations on the word, column, and page counts of the 1623 Folio, and a message surfacing word by word to the effect that Bacon wrote the plays and hid the fact where only patience would ever find it.
suggested_refs: Francis Bacon's biliteral cipher, set out in De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623), the historical hook the Cryptogram exploits
William and Elizebeth Friedman, The Shakespearean Ciphers Examined (1957), which finds no such cipher in the text
sources: Open Library edition records for The Great Cryptogram

stops.name: Fetter Lane, London, Sampson Low
stops.date_confidence: attested that he travelled to England to arrange the English publication of the book by Sampson Low (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). Coordinates are St. Dunstan's House, Fetter Lane, the firm's address from 1887, per Wikipedia, 'Sampson Low'; the Paternoster Row address often given belongs to a later period of the firm. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He crosses to England to arrange the English edition with Sampson Low, whose house stands at St. Dunstan's in Fetter Lane, a few steps off Fleet Street. He is fifty-six, out of office, and in the one season of his life when the world is prepared to hear him as a scholar. The American reviews are already bad. He does not read them as a verdict, he reads them as the ordinary resistance of men whose profession he has walked around, and he books the halls.
suggested_refs: The Sampson Low, Marston, Searle and Rivington edition of The Great Cryptogram, London, 1888

stops.name: London, the tour of England, Scotland, and Ireland
stops.date_confidence: attested that he toured England, Scotland, and Ireland lecturing and debating the theory (MNopedia). No itinerary, venues, or dates were found for the tour, so the pin is London as its base and the month is an ordering device. That his father emigrated from Fintona, County Tyrone, is attested (Wikipedia); that Donnelly had not previously seen Ireland is inference.
stops.campa: He lectures across England, Scotland, and Ireland: the Folio held up, the numbers read out, the arithmetic performed in front of audiences who have come to see whether the American is a crank or a discoverer. The press handles him as a spectacle first and an argument second, which is the order in which he is handled from here to the end. His father left County Tyrone before he was born, and this is the first time he stands on the island. The halls fill.
suggested_refs: English and Scottish press notices of Donnelly's 1888 lecture tour

stops.name: Oxford Union, the motion put
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly' states that he spoke at the Oxford and Cambridge Unions, where his thesis, 'Resolved, that the works of William Shakespeare were composed by Francis Bacon', was put to an unsuccessful vote. An earlier pass over the same article failed to find the passage and wrongly downgraded it to tradition; that downgrade is withdrawn. The exact date is not given by the source and is an ordering device. Coordinates are the Union at Frewin Court per Wikipedia, 'Oxford Union'.
stops.campa: At the Oxford Union the motion is put in form: Resolved, that the works of William Shakespeare were composed by Francis Bacon. The wording is his own thesis, carried over from the book. Donnelly speaks for it in the chamber at Frewin Court, before undergraduates who have read enough of the plays to argue and enough of the newspapers to be sceptical. He is given the whole courtesy of the forms he came to be judged under: the debate, the division, the count. Then the house divides and the motion is lost.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Union order books for the 1888 term, which would give the date and the division figures

stops.name: Cambridge Union, the same motion
stops.date_confidence: attested by the same sentence in Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly' that covers Oxford; the article treats the two Unions together and gives no separate date, so the date here only orders the pair. Coordinates are 9A Bridge Street per Wikipedia, 'Cambridge Union Society'.
stops.campa: At the Cambridge Union in Bridge Street the same motion is put and goes the same way. Two ancient debating societies have now heard the cipher explained by the man who found it, and both have voted that it is not there. In America the book has already sold poorly and been mauled in the reviews; in England it has been refuted by a show of hands in the two rooms most likely to have decided for him. He withdraws nothing. He leaves Cambridge and goes on with the tour, the two volumes under his arm and the arithmetic unaltered.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Union Society records for 1888

stops.name: Stratford-upon-Avon, Henley Street
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weak. No source names a visit to Stratford. It is inferred only from the documented England, Scotland, and Ireland tour (MNopedia) and the obviousness of the errand. Kept as tradition and marked as such rather than dropped or asserted; the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Tradition puts him on Henley Street, at the house where the man he says wrote nothing was born. No source names the visit and he never describes it, but the tour carries him within a day of Stratford and the newspapers of that season expect the errand of him. If he stood in that room, he stood in front of the one class of evidence his method could not process: a house, a birth, a name in a parish register, and nothing in any of it to count. The record is silent on whether he went, and silent on what he made of it.
suggested_refs: Shakespeare's Birthplace, Henley Street, Stratford-upon-Avon

segments.name: Caesar's Column and the Omaha Preamble

stops.name: Nininger, the post office discontinued
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Nininger post office closed in 1889 after thirty-three years of operation (Wikipedia, 'Nininger, Minnesota'). Those two figures put its opening in 1856, before Donnelly reached the Territory, so the common gloss that it opened with his town is wrong and is not repeated here. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Nininger's post office, opened in 1856 and kept through thirty-three years of the town's slow evacuation, is discontinued. What was platted as a city is now a farm district with a name on it. He has lived inside the ruin of his own promotional literature for thirty-two years and will live in it twelve more. He stays on in the farmhouse, which with the Good Templars Hall is the last thing of consequence left standing in the place. His mail comes through Hastings from now on.
suggested_refs: The two historical plaques at Nininger, marking Good Templars Hall and the site of Donnelly's residence

stops.name: Chicago, Caesar's Column
stops.date_confidence: attested; published 1890 by F. J. Schulte and Company, Chicago, under the pseudonym Edmund Boisgilbert, M.D., selling roughly 60,000 copies on first release and some 250,000 in all (Wikipedia, 'Caesar's Column'). Month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinates are city-level.
stops.campa: F. J. Schulte of Chicago publishes Caesar's Column: A Story of the Twentieth Century, by Edmund Boisgilbert, M.D. The doctor is Donnelly, hiding from his own reputation. The novel is set in the New York of 1988, a city of airships and electric light owned outright by a plutocracy, where the rising of the workers, when it comes, is not a revolution but a massacre, and the dead are stacked in a column of concrete as a monument to it. Sixty thousand copies go at once and a quarter of a million in all.
suggested_refs: Caesar's Column: A Story of the Twentieth Century (Chicago: F. J. Schulte and Company, 1890)

stops.name: St. Paul, the state Senate again
stops.date_confidence: attested; Minnesota Senate, 24th district, 5 January 1891 to 6 January 1895 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). Coordinates are the second capitol on the Wabasha Hill site, in use 1883-1905.
stops.campa: He is elected to the state Senate once more, from the twenty-fourth district, to the second capitol on the hill where the first one burned. He is sixty. In these same months the farmers' organizations of the West and the South are converging, meeting by meeting, on the idea of a national party of their own, and the man they will ask to write its language is a Minnesota state senator with a comet book and a Shakespeare cipher already against his name. He sits from January 1891 to January 1895.
suggested_refs: The Minnesota Farmers' Alliance and its convergence on third-party politics, 1890-1892

stops.name: Nininger, two novels
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1891 for Doctor Huguet and 1892 for The Golden Bottle from the bibliography in Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; months unknown and the date is an ordering device. The plot summaries are from the novels themselves; place of composition is inferred from his Nininger residence.
stops.campa: Doctor Huguet appears in 1891 and The Golden Bottle in 1892. In the first, a white Southern gentleman wakes in the body of a black field hand and lives out what that costs, written by a man who voted for the Freedmen's Bureau twenty-five years before and has not changed his mind since. In the second, a Kansas farm boy is given a bottle that turns iron into gold and remakes the finance of the world with it. The novels and the platform work are one argument in two kinds of clothing. He is sixty, sitting in the state Senate, and writing the fiction between sessions.
suggested_refs: Doctor Huguet (1891) and The Golden Bottle (1892)

stops.name: St. Louis, the Industrial Conference
stops.date_confidence: attested; at the St. Louis reform convention of February 1892 Donnelly delivered the closing speech and the delegates resolved to form the People's Party (Wikipedia, 'People's Party (United States)'). Exact day not given and defaulted. The number of participating organizations is the standard figure for the conference and is [R] as sourced here.
stops.campa: Twenty-two reform organizations meet at St. Louis to decide whether to become a party. The Alliance men, the Knights of Labor, the greenbackers, the silver men: each with a grievance and none with a ticket. He is sixty years old and has lost more elections than he has won, and he is handed the language of a national movement because nobody in the hall writes it better. Donnelly gives the closing speech, and the delegates resolve to found the People's Party before they go home.
stops.quote: We meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, closing speech to the Industrial Conference, St. Louis, February 1892, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'People's Party (United States)'; the same sentence opens the Omaha Platform preamble five months later
suggested_refs: The St. Louis Industrial Conference of February 1892 and its resolutions

stops.name: Omaha, the preamble on the Fourth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested; Donnelly wrote the preamble to the Omaha Platform, adopted at the People's Party national convention on 4 July 1892 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; Wikipedia, 'People's Party (United States)'). The quotation follows the American Presidency Project and Wikisource transcriptions, which read 'grand general and chief'; Wikipedia's 'Omaha Platform' article carries a 'chieftain' variant not found in the authoritative texts.
stops.campa: At Omaha the People's Party adopts its platform, and the preamble is his: the graduated income tax, the direct election of senators, the sub-treasury plan, public ownership of the railroads, the whole of it introduced by a paragraph that reads like scripture and was written by a novelist. Every measure in the document is called visionary by the newspapers of 1892. Most of them are law within thirty years, carried by men who would not have shaken his hand. The convention does its business on the Fourth of July.
stops.quote: Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of "the plain people," with which class it originated.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, preamble to the People's Party (Omaha) Platform, adopted Omaha, Nebraska, 4 July 1892; text per the American Presidency Project, following Porter and Johnson, National Party Platforms, and Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Omaha Platform of the People's Party, 4 July 1892

stops.name: St. Paul, the governorship lost
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia, '1892 Minnesota gubernatorial election' gives Donnelly (Populist) 39,862 votes, 15.58 percent, against Knute Nelson (Republican) 109,220, 42.68 percent, on 8 November 1892. Compilations placing his gubernatorial run in 1900 are wrong: he is not a candidate in Wikipedia's 1900 Minnesota returns. An MNopedia claim of an 1888 run is likewise unsupported by the 1888 returns.
stops.campa: He runs for governor of Minnesota on the Populist ticket in the autumn of the same year and takes 39,862 votes, fifteen and a half percent, against Knute Nelson's 109,220. The preamble read aloud in reform halls from Kansas to Georgia does not carry his own state. He writes the words other men win with, and the pattern is old enough by now that he shows no sign of resenting it. Four months after Omaha he is back at Nininger, sixty-one years old, with a Senate seat and a farm that has never paid.
suggested_refs: Minnesota gubernatorial returns, 8 November 1892

stops.name: Nininger, the death of Katherine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); month, day, and place of death are not given by the sources checked, and the Nininger pin is his standing residence rather than an attested location. Nothing was found on how he responded to it.
stops.campa: Katherine McCaffrey Donnelly dies after thirty-nine years of marriage, the whole of it spent in a town that failed in its first season. She came out from Philadelphia to a levee city that existed on an engraving, and stayed on in the farm that stood where the engraving had put warehouses. Three children. The sources give the year and give nothing else: no month, no place, no account of the funeral, and no line from him about her in anything he publishes afterward. He is sixty-two, and alone in the farmhouse.
suggested_refs: The Donnelly family papers at the Minnesota Historical Society, which hold the diaries the published record omits

stops.name: Nininger, silver and the last cipher
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1896 for The Bryan Campaign for the American People's Money and 1899 for The Cipher in the Plays, and on the Tombstone, from the bibliography in Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'. The two are combined in one stop; months unknown and defaulted. The reading of fusion as the dissolution of the People's Party is standard interpretation, not a sourced claim about Donnelly's own view.
stops.campa: In 1896 he writes The Bryan Campaign for the American People's Money, throwing the Populist weight behind free silver and the Democratic nominee, which is the same decision that dissolves the party into the party it was founded to replace. Three years later he publishes The Cipher in the Plays, and on the Tombstone, still counting, still certain, answering the reviewers of 1888 as though the debate at Oxford had merely been adjourned. He is sixty-seven and has changed his mind about nothing.
suggested_refs: The Cipher in the Plays, and on the Tombstone (1899), his last Baconian work

stops.name: St. Paul, the last office
stops.date_confidence: attested; Minnesota House of Representatives, 24th district, 4 January 1897 to 1 January 1899 (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). The tally of offices and defeats in the campa is assembled from the same article's officeholding record; the count of defeats is not given as a total anywhere in the sources.
stops.campa: At sixty-five he is returned once more to the Minnesota House, from the twenty-fourth district, for two years. It is the last office he holds. Set end to end the record runs: lieutenant governor, three terms in Congress, two in the state Senate, two in the House, and defeats scattered at every level in between, beginning with the two legislative races he lost in 1857 and 1858, in the mud of a town that had just stopped selling. This last term runs from January 1897 to January 1899.
suggested_refs: Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, officeholding record for Ignatius Donnelly

stops.name: Nininger, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: the marriage to Marian Hanson, his secretary, in 1898 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); month, day, and place are not, and the Nininger pin is inferred from his standing residence. Her age is not stated in the sources checked and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Four years a widower, at sixty-six, he marries Marian Hanson, who has been his secretary. Minnesota talks about it. Neither the day nor the place of the ceremony is recorded in anything reachable, though he is living at Nininger and has lived nowhere else since he came into the Territory in 1857. He has two years and some months left, and he spends them the way he has spent the last forty, at the desk in the morning and on the platform when anybody asks.
suggested_refs: The Donnelly correspondence at the Minnesota Historical Society

stops.name: Cincinnati, nominated for Vice President
stops.date_confidence: attested; the anti-fusion Populists met at Cincinnati in May 1900 and nominated Wharton Barker for President with Donnelly for Vice President, and the ticket lost the general election (Wikipedia, 'Wharton Barker'; Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'). Exact day defaulted. The vote share is not quoted from a source here beyond its being a small fraction.
stops.campa: The Populists who will not fuse with the Democrats meet at Cincinnati and put up a ticket of their own: Wharton Barker of Pennsylvania for President and Ignatius Donnelly for Vice President of the United States. It is what is left of the party he named at St. Louis eight years earlier, running chiefly to demonstrate that it still exists. He campaigns for it through the autumn, sixty-eight years old, on trains and in halls, and in November the ticket takes a fraction of a percent.
suggested_refs: The Cincinnati convention of the anti-fusion People's Party, May 1900

stops.name: Minneapolis, the first day of the century
stops.date_confidence: attested that he died at Minneapolis on 1 January 1901, aged sixty-nine (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'; MNopedia). The tradition that he collapsed after giving a New Year's toast is widely repeated and is not attested in any source checked this session; it is stated here as tradition and not as fact.
stops.campa: He dies at Minneapolis on the first day of 1901, sixty-nine years old, at the opening of the century whose New York he had already written as a plutocracy with a column of the dead standing in it. He had been on trains through the autumn, campaigning for a ticket that took a fraction of a percent. Tradition holds that he collapsed after proposing a New Year's toast; the tradition is not attested anywhere the sources reach. What is certain is the date, the first of January, 1901.
suggested_refs: Minneapolis and St. Paul obituary notices, January 1901

stops.name: Calvary Cemetery, St. Paul, the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested that he is buried at Calvary Cemetery, St. Paul (Wikipedia, 'Ignatius L. Donnelly'); the day of burial is not given and is an ordering device. Coordinates are 753 Front Avenue per Wikipedia, 'Calvary Cemetery (St. Paul, Minnesota)'. Wikipedia's own roster of notable burials there does not list him, and no description of a headstone was found; a FindAGrave lookup returned a blocked page. That the papers are at the Minnesota Historical Society is attested by MNHS; the often-quoted 1812-1973 date span for the collection could not be verified.
stops.campa: He is buried at Calvary Cemetery on Front Avenue, a few miles up the bluff from the levee where he first landed in the Territory. His papers, letters, speeches, diaries, and manuscripts go to the Minnesota Historical Society, where the man the newspapers filed under cranks becomes a collection with a finding aid. No description of the headstone survives in anything reachable, and the cemetery's own roll of notable burials leaves him off it. Atlantis has not been out of print since 1882.
stops.quote: Further investigations and discoveries will, I trust, confirm the correctness of the conclusions at which I have arrived.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Chapter I (Project Gutenberg ebook 4032)
suggested_refs: The Ignatius Donnelly papers, Minnesota Historical Society, St. Paul
Jason Colavito on Atlantis: The Antediluvian World as 'the platonic ideal of fringe history'
